messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 65
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Project Manager
- Trauma Type: Child's life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 46

He is 65, a widowed man from Oceania who has spent most of his adult life working as a project manager, the sort of person who calms rooms by drawing timelines on whiteboards and breaking impossible things into steps. When he speaks about the worst period of his life, though, that habit of ordering events begins to fail him. He starts with the hospital.

His son is eight when he becomes critically ill. What begins as a fever and vomiting turns, over a few frightening days, into an emergency transfer, intensive care, and the kind of medical language that makes a parent feel both desperate and useless. He remembers the fluorescent lights, the cold vinyl chair beside the bed, the hiss and alarm of machines. He remembers the consultant speaking carefully, trying not to promise anything. Most of all he remembers his son’s face, swollen and pale, almost unrecognizable, and the shock of seeing a child’s body attached to tubes and lines meant to keep him alive.

At first he goes into action. He keeps a notebook in his shirt pocket and writes down every blood result, every medication change, every name of every doctor on shift. He updates family members, organizes meals, answers work emails from the corridor, and tells himself that if he stays useful he will not fall apart. Nurses compliment how steady he seems. Inside, he is braced every second for someone to come through the doors and tell him his son has died.

The illness stretches on for weeks. He sleeps in fragments, shoes on, waking at each change in the monitor’s rhythm. He becomes frightened of leaving the unit even to shower or get coffee, convinced something catastrophic will happen in the ten minutes he is gone. Once, while he is downstairs paying for tea, a code alarm sounds somewhere in the hospital. His body goes cold before his mind catches up, and he runs back toward the ward, certain it is his son. He can still feel that sprint in his chest when he talks about it now.

His son survives, but the relief never lands cleanly. Even after discharge, he lives as if danger is still crouched just out of sight. At home he checks on the boy repeatedly through the night, holding his breath near the bedroom door to hear whether he is breathing. If his son sleeps later than usual, he is instantly flooded with dread. Childhood colds, stomach aches, and school absences become emergencies in his mind before there is any evidence that they are. He tries not to show it, but his fear leaks out as irritability and control. He pushes for second opinions, tracks symptoms obsessively, and snaps at anyone who tells him he is overreacting.

Around the same time, his wife develops her own health problems years later and eventually dies, a loss he speaks about softly, as if lowering his voice might keep it contained. Since her death, the old fear around his son’s illness seems to have sharpened rather than faded. He says widowhood took away the one person who truly understood those hospital nights. Without her, memories come back with less warning and less buffer.

In his job, he is respected for being dependable, but the qualities that once made him excellent now seem fused to vigilance. He arrives early, triple-checks risk registers, and feels a surge of anger when colleagues are casual about deadlines or contingency plans. If a team member says, “It’ll probably be fine,” he feels his jaw tighten. “Probably” is not reassuring to him. He has lived through the day when everything was supposed to be fine until it was not. When projects run into trouble, he notices his body reacting before his thoughts do—heart racing, shoulders rigid, a hot pressure behind his eyes—as though he is back outside intensive care waiting for bad news.

He avoids the pediatric wing of the hospital where his son was treated, even though it would be the quickest route to visit another clinic in the same complex. Medical dramas on television are turned off within minutes. The beeping of checkout scanners or reversing trucks can trigger a jolt of panic because they echo the cadence of monitors. At night he still dreams that he is walking into his son’s hospital room and finding the bed empty, or that he cannot get through a corridor no matter how fast he runs. He wakes disoriented, drenched in sweat, then lies still listening for sounds in the house.

His son is an adult now. He knows, rationally, that the crisis is long over. He is even proud of the life his son has built. But when his son does not answer a text for several hours, his mind fills in disaster with vivid precision. He imagines emergency rooms, phone calls, white sheets, and that old impossible helplessness. He hates how quickly his imagination goes there, hates even more that part of him still believes constant vigilance is the only thing standing between love and catastrophe.

He describes himself as tired—tired of scanning, tired of bracing, tired of carrying images that feel more present than memories should. He wants to remember his son’s childhood without seeing tubes, machines, and fluorescent light. But the story of being his son’s father still keeps folding back to that hospital room, as if some part of him never fully left it.
